row.name: The Pipers
row.description: The Pipers are a pair of standing stones near The Hurlers stone circles, located on Bodmin Moor near the village of Minions, Cornwall [1]. The Pipers are approximately 2 metres high and the width between them is about the same distance [1]. They are situated about 120 metres west-south-west of the central Hurlers circle [1]. According to folklore they represent musicians playing for three circles of dancers who were turned to stone for engaging in festivities on a holy day [1].

row.name: Y Garn Goch
row.description: Y Garn Goch is a hill in the Brecon Beacons National Park in the east of Carmarthenshire, Wales [1]. The name means the 'red cairn' [1]. It lies near the village of Bethlehem, three miles southwest of Llangadog and four miles east of Llandeilo on the southern side of the broad Towy Valley [1]. It is also commonly known as either Garn Goch or Carn Goch [1]. The established view is that Y Garn Goch is notable for the two impressive Iron Age hillforts of Y Gaer Fawr, (English: the big fort) and Y Gaer Fach, (English: the little fort), together the largest in southern Wales [1].

row.name: Lopen Roman Mosaic
row.description: The Lopen Roman Mosaic is a Roman mosaic, probably from a Roman villa, in the village of Lopen, Somerset, England [1]. Photogrammetry by English Heritage was followed by excavation led by the Somerset County Council archaeologist [1]. The stones used for the mosaic are Blue Lias from the surrounding hills [1]. A further mosaic was found in an adjoining room, which probably extended beyond the area excavated, which was about 4.5 metres square [1]. The main mosaic is almost 7 metres square and has a complicated geometrical design, including some stylized figurative elements such as leaves, cups and dolphins [1].

row.name: Etruscan Pyramid of Bomarzo
row.description: A megalithic rock-cut monument carved from a single block of volcanic tuff near Viterbo, Italy [1] [2] [3]. Dating to the 7th-6th century BC, the pyramid is believed to have served as an Etruscan sacrificial altar used by haruspices for divination rituals [1] [4]. Channels carved into the rock may have drained liquids during animal sacrifices [1] [4]. The site was rediscovered near the famous Sacred Grove of Bomarzo [3] [4].

row.name: Ringsbury Camp
row.description: An Iron Age multivallate hillfort dating to approximately 50 BC in the parish of Purton, Wiltshire [1] [2]. The scheduled monument encloses 3.4 hectares within double banks: the inner bank rises 5 metres high surrounded by a 3-metre ditch, while the outer bank stands 2 metres high [1]. The banks are built from non-local limestone rubble, suggesting transported material [1] [2]. Neolithic flint tools and an Iron Age coin (now in Purton Museum) have also been found at the site [1].

row.name: Samsø
row.description: Samsø is a Danish island in the Kattegat 15 kilometers off the Jutland Peninsula [1]. Due to its central location, the island was used during the Viking Age as a meeting place [1]. People have lived and hunted on Samsø since the ice receded at the end of the last Ice Age [1]. Excavations at Tønnesminde and Endebjerg show evidence of human habitation from the Stone Age through the Viking Age [1]. A canal was dug across the island at its narrowest place [1]. The canal was about 500 m long and 11 m wide and could in its time be navigated by vessels with a draught of up to 1 m [1]. It was dug and clad with wooden linings in the years 726–729 AD; the last part of the Scandinavian Iron Age [1].

row.name: Cefn Bryn
row.description: Cefn Bryn is an ancient ridge in Britain [1]. It is a 5-mile-long Old Red Sandstone ridge in south Wales, in the heart of the Gower Peninsula [1]. Just north of the ridge summit of Cefn Bryn, there is a Neolithic burial ground, known as "Arthur's Stone" [1]. Beneath the bracken on the hill over sixty cairns have been discovered [1]. Most of these are likely to be no more than collections of stones cleared by local farmers; but just north-west of Arthur's Stone three prominent cairns have been excavated that prove their ancient role - the largest being Great Cairn, a circular heap of stones above a central grave [1].

row.name: Goyet Caves
row.description: The Goyet Caves are a series of connected caves located in Belgium in a limestone cliff about 15 m above the river Samson near the village of Mozet in the Gesves municipality of the Namur province [1]. Occasional Neanderthal occupation begins 120,000 years ago and ends after 40,000 years ago [1]. Between 45,500 and 40,500 years ago Neanderthals lived in the Troisième Caverne, where 99 bones were discovered, that belong to at least five individuals [1]. This represents the largest collection of Neanderthal fossils in Northern Europe [1]. The condition of the fossils strongly suggests cannibalism [1]. Homo sapiens occupation began around 35,000 years ago [1]. The 35,000 year old humerus of a man from Goyet has been associated with the Aurignacian culture [1].

row.name: Bury Camp
row.description: Bury Camp is the site of an Iron Age multivallate hillfort in north-west Wiltshire, England [1]. It occupies a triangular promontory of Colerne Down, in the north of Colerne parish, at the southern edge of the Cotswold Hills between two spurs of a river valley [1]. The enclosed area of approximately 9.2ha is surrounded by a ditch 4m wide and up to 1m deep, and an outer rampart up to 1.5m high on the east and northwestern sides and up to 2m high on the southwestern side, across the neck of the promontory [1]. The building of the hillfort can be dated to about 350 BC, but various Neolithic and Mesolithic flint tools were found, indicating a much earlier use [1]. In 1960, 175 shards of pottery were recovered; all except one were plain coarse ware without a trace of decoration [1]. Among organic remains, only two fragments of human bones were found, whereas between 400 and 500 animal bone fragments were found [1].

row.name: Barbar Temple
row.description: The Barbar Temple is an archaeological site located in the village of Barbar, Bahrain, considered to be part of the Dilmun culture [1]. The most recent of the three Barbar temples was rediscovered by a Danish archaeological team in 1954 [1]. A further two temples were discovered on the site with the oldest dating back to 3000 BC [1]. The three temples were built atop one another with the second built approximately 500 years later and the third added between 2100 BC and 2000 BC [1]. It is thought that the temples were constructed to worship the god Enki, the god of wisdom and freshwater, and his wife Nankhur Sak (Ninhursag) [1]. During the excavation of the site many tools, weapons, pottery and small pieces of gold were found which are now on display in the Bahrain National Museum [1]. The most famous find was a copper bull's head [1].

row.name: La Garma Cave Complex
row.description: The La Garma cave complex is a parietal art-bearing paleoanthropological cave system in Cantabria, Spain [1]. The cave complex is noted for one of the best preserved floors from the Paleolithic containing more than 4,000 fossils and more than 500 graphical units [1]. The Lower Gallery of La Garma is situated at 59 m above sea level and is around 300 m in length [1]. It was discovered in November 1995 [1]. Its original entrance was sealed during the Pleistocene by a rockslide about 16,000 years ago, preserving the cave floor in a pristine manner [1]. La Garma is notable for its rich repository of Magdalenian portable art found in The Lower Gallery [1]. The most outstanding artefact is a backward-facing ibex depiction carved onto a bovine rib spatula [1]. The peculiar remains of five Visigothic youths were found deep in the cave system [1].

row.name: Tholos de Montelirio
row.description: Tholos de Montelirio is an archaeological site in Seville Province, Spain, at Valencina de la Concepción [1]. Tholos de Montelirio is closed to the general public, but its objects can be viewed in the Archeological Museum of Seville [1]. A Bayesian model based on 22 radiocarbon dates on human bone suggested that the use of Tholos de Montelirio started in 2875–2700 BC and ended in 2805–2635 BC [1].

row.name: Carwynnen Quoit
row.description: Carwynnen Quoit is a dolmen belonging to the Neolithic period, at Carwynnen near Camborne in west Cornwall [1]. It is also known as 'The Giant's Quoit', 'The Giant's Frying Pan', 'Pendarvis Quoit' and 'Pendarves Quoit' [1]. It collapsed in 1966 and was re-erected in 2014 [1]. Carwynnen Quoit is one of an ancient and rare group of monuments and can be found at Carwynnen in Cornwall [1]. It is a portal dolmen belonging to the Neolithic period, built around 3000 BC, one of the few Cornish portal dolmens to be found outside the Penwith peninsula [1]. It is situated on a gentle west-facing slope between two small tributaries to the Red River [1]. The dolmen stands to a height of 1.5 metres with a capstone measuring around 3.3 metres long by 2.5 metres wide and 30 cm thick and weighs around 10 tons [1]. The site was first recorded by the Welsh antiquarian Edward Lhuyd around 1700 and a symbol of the cromlech appeared on Martyn's 1748 map of Cornwall [1].

row.name: Borkowo Megalithic Cemetery
row.description: Borkowo megalithic cemetery is a prehistoric burial ground situated in the county of Sławno, in Western Pomerania [1]. The site consists of a passage grave, unchambered long barrows, and other tumuli [1]. The most impressive monument, Borkowo 1, is a passage grave made with heavy boulders and capstones [1]. It is around 4.5 metres long, with a width of 1.5 metres [1]. Excavations revealed a cremation and a few pottery sherds [1]. The grave is assigned to the Funnelbeaker culture of the Chalcolithic Age [1].

row.name: Boralday Archaeological Site
row.description: Boralday, is a kurgan necropolis in Almaty, Kazakhstan, dating to the early Iron Age and associated with the Saka people [1]. The necropolis comprises 430 hectares and includes 47 mounds from the Saka period from the 5th to the 3rd centuries BC [1]. The height of the largest mound, which is located in the center of the necropolis, is 14 meters, and the diameter is 100 meters [1]. There are also several mounds with a height of 5–6 meters and a diameter of 60–80 meters [1]. Medium-sized mounds have a height of 3 meters and a diameter of 30–40 meters, and the small ones have a height of 1–1,5 meters and a diameter of 10–20 meters [1].

row.name: Inka Tunuwiri
row.description: Inka Tunuwiri (Hispanicized: Incatunuhuiri) is an archaeological site in Peru's Puno Region, located between the districts of Chucuito and Puno, southeast of the village Ichu [1]. The site features a pyramidal hill with sandstone walls, stone monoliths carved in human form, and terraces [2]. Evidence suggests occupation dating to the Pukara culture (500 BC-400 AD), with structural parallels to Pucara in Lampa Province [2]. The Ichu community considers it a sacred ceremonial center where Pachamama offerings are performed during carnival season [2]. The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage of Peru [1].

row.name: Temple of Artemis - Sardes
row.description: The fourth largest Ionic temple in the ancient world, located in the ruins of Sardis, capital of ancient Lydia in western Turkey [1] [2]. Construction began in the Hellenistic period around 300 BC and was significantly reworked under Emperor Hadrian in the mid-2nd century AD, when the cella was divided into chambers for both Artemis and the Imperial cult [1] [3]. The pseudodipteros temple measures approximately 44.6 by 97.6 metres with eight columns on each end [1]. Only two of the original columns remained standing [1] [4].

row.name: Bull of the Corcyreans
row.description: The Bull of the Corcyreans was a bronze statue dedicated around 480 BC by the citizens of Corcyra (modern Corfu) at the Sanctuary of Apollo in Delphi, Greece [1] [2]. According to Pausanias, a bull in Corfu repeatedly went to the shore and moaned; when the herdsman investigated, he found the sea teeming with tuna [1] [3]. After consulting the Delphic Oracle and sacrificing a bull to Poseidon, the Corcyreans made an enormous catch and dedicated the statue with a tithe of the proceeds [1] [4]. The sculptor was Theopropus of Aegina [1] [3]. Only the base survives, visible on the right side just past the sanctuary entrance along the Sacred Way [1] [2].

row.name: Atzompa
row.description: Zapotec elite residential complex located 4 km north of Monte Alban in Oaxaca, occupied during periods IIIB-IV (c. 650-850 AD) [1] [2] [3]. The site features high-status palatial units including the House of Altars and House of the East, along with three Mesoamerican ballcourts, the largest measuring 45 by 22 metres -- the biggest in all of Monte Alban [1] [3]. Excavations beginning in 2007 uncovered effigy vessels and funerary urns demonstrating advanced Zapotec craftsmanship [1] [3] [4] [5]. The name derives from Nahuatl meaning "at the water's head" [3].

row.card: Occupied 650–850 AD on a hilltop above Monte Albán, this satellite city supplied quarried stone to the larger centre below and produced the green-glazed pottery traded as far as Teotihuacan.

row.name: Halliggye Fogou
row.description: Halliggye Fogou is one of many fogous in Cornwall, England [1]. The Halliggye Fogou consists of a long narrow tunnel leading to three sectioned chambers [1]. The complex of passages has a roof and walls of stone, and is the largest and best-preserved of several mysterious tunnels associated with Cornish Iron Age settlements [1]. Pottery found during excavations has included local Iron Age cordoned wares and some sherds of Roman Samian ware from southern Gaul [1].

row.name: Cadbury Hill
row.description: Cadbury Hill is a small hill, mostly in the civil parish of Congresbury, overlooking the village of Yatton in North Somerset [1]. On its summit stands an Iron Age hill fort, which is a Scheduled Ancient Monument [1]. In archaeological circles, the hill fort is known as Cadbury-Congresbury in order to differentiate it from the Cadbury Castle hillfort in South Cadbury [1]. It appears to have been constructed in the Iron Age when one or more ramparts, with walls and ditches, were built on the steep slopes of the hill to defend an area covering some eight and a half acres [1]. The remains of Iron Age round houses may still be seen inside [1]. The hill fort was refortified around 400, after the urban collapse associated with the withdrawal of Rome, and occupation extended into the sub-Roman period [1].

row.name: Uqair Salt Mine Archaeological Site
row.description: A Hellenistic-period archaeological site located approximately 25 km northwest of Uqair in al-Hasa, Eastern Saudi Arabia [1]. Surface remains include walls 10-30 cm high and extensive irrigation works visible on aerial photographs [1] [2]. A Danish archaeological team in 1968 discovered building remains and pottery sherds comparable to types from Thaj and Hellenistic Bahrain [1] [2]. The site is associated with the ancient port city of Uqair on the Persian Gulf coast, linked to the classical city of Gerrha mentioned by Greek and Roman sources [1] [2].

row.name: Peqin Castle
row.description: The Peqin Castle is a ruined Ottoman Turkish castle in Peqin, Albania [1]. The foundations of the castle are thought to date from the Roman period, the time of the construction of the Via Egnatia [1]. Its walls at one point had a height of around 12 metres [1]. The castle was later rebuilt and expanded during the Turkish occupation of Albania, at which time it was passed into the control of the Sipahi of the local fief, who added a palace and a harem [1]. The last resident of the castle was Demir Pasha [1]. The castle was equipped with tunnels which served as exits several km away from the city in difficult times [1]. Clay pipes have been found in the walls of the castle, which archaeologists believe is an indication that water was supplied from outside the castle during wartime [1].

row.name: Foel Fenlli
row.description: Foel Fenlli or Moel Fenlli is a hill in Denbighshire, North Wales [1]. With a summit at an elevation of 511 metres, it is the second highest peak of the Clwydian Range [1]. The remains of a hillfort roughly 25 acres in area are found on the peak [1]. According to later legend recorded in the Historia Brittonum the "iniquitous and tyrannical" king Benlli probably lived there c. 450 [1]. He was admonished for opposing Saint Germanus, and he and his castle were "consumed by fire from heaven", so the legend goes [1]. There are the remains of strong ramparts on all sides, with an entrance at the west end [1]. In the south-west quarter of the fort enclosure are about two dozen hut platforms; there is a spring close to the centre [1].

row.name: Mongchontoseong Earthen Fortification
row.description: Mongchontoseong is an ancient earthen rampart dating from the Baekje period [1]. The fortification walls are estimated to have been about 2.7 km in length and approximately 6 to 7 m high [1]. The fortifications of Mongch'ont'osŏng had a palisade atop the wall and a moat surrounding its base [1]. They are part of Wiryeseong with Pungnaptoseong [1]. A number of important excavations of the site were conducted prior to the construction of the nearby Olympic Park [1].

row.name: King John's Hill
row.description: King John's Hill is the site of an Iron Age hillfort located in Hampshire, in southeast England [1]. King John's Hill is a small multivallate hillfort, a fort with multiple defensive rings, and has been dated on ceramic evidence to approximately 100 BC [1]. The hill rises 129 metres above mean sea level and is just over 0.5 kilometres southeast of the village of East Worldham, and approximately 4 kilometres east of the town of Alton [1]. The hillfort is unusually small, and its defences were weak; the site falls in a borderline category between larger hillforts and smaller defended settlements [1]. It is oval in shape and encloses an area of approximately 0.8 hectares [1]. The hill was partially excavated in 1939 and 1947 [1]. Ceramic fragments dating to the Iron Age were recovered, and two infilled storage pits were discovered [1]. A ring-headed pin, fashioned from wire, was recovered from one of the Iron Age storage pits [1].

row.name: Breitenbach - Archaeological Site
row.description: The archaeological site near the village of Breitenbach in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany is an important open-air settlement that dates to the period of initial colonization of Europe by anatomically modern humans [1]. The occupations date to the early Upper Palaeolithic and more specifically belong to the Aurignacian cultural complex [1]. Breitenbach is currently the biggest open-air settlement site in western Eurasia dating to this time period [1]. Overlying the Palaleolithic deposits are the remains of a younger settlement that has been dated to the Neolithic [1]. The site was discovered in the spring of 1925 by the local school teacher E. Thiersch [1]. Several 14C dates place the occupations at Breitenbach between 23,990±180 and 28,380±170 years ago [1]. The site is primarily known for its mammoth remains [1]. Also occurring in numbers at the site are the remains of horse, reindeer and to a lesser extent those of woolly rhinoceros, hyena, wolf, lion, Arctic fox and Arctic hare [1].

row.name: Grubstones
row.description: The Grubstones circle is located on Burley Moor [1]. The circle is just over 800 metres south-east of the Twelve Apostles [1]. The circle has a diameter of about 10 metres [1]. It is almost perfectly circular with twenty surviving stones [1]. The stones are set on the inside of a low bank, about 1.8 metres wide [1]. The circle has been described variously as a cairn circle, a ring cairn enclosure, or a stone circle [1]. One third of the circle on the south side has been destroyed by shooting butts [1].

row.name: Berry Mound
row.description: Berry Mound is an Iron Age hill fort in the Bromsgrove district of Worcestershire, near Shirley, West Midlands, on the outskirts of Birmingham [1]. It has been dated to the 1st or 2nd century BC [1]. To the north was a V-shaped ditch that was 15 ft wide and 6 ft deep, to the south one 22 ft wide and 7 ft deep [1]. Faint traces of a second rampart or defensive terrace to the north were observed in 1959, and 19th century observers recorded the existence of a third line of ramparts and ditches, though no traces of these remain [1]. The entrance to the fort was on the east side, though it is possible that there was originally a second entrance located on an axis with the first, as at the similar Sutton Walls Hill Fort [1]. The site was excavated in 1959, with traces of timber revetments being found on the ramparts [1].

row.name: Mausoleum of Tangun
row.description: The Mausoleum of Tangun is an ancient burial site in Kangdong near Pyongyang, North Korea [1]. It is claimed by North Korea to be the tomb of Tangun, founder of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom [1]. A pyramid was built on top of the grave in 1994, consisting of 1994 blocks of stone [1]. The complex occupies about 1.8 km² on the slope of Mount Taebak [1]. A nail found in the mausoleum, dating to the Goguryeo period, has been the subject of much controversy [1]. This discovery has thus led some North Korean historians to conclude that the mausoleum was discovered and renovated during that period [1]. South Korean historians think it's more likely to be a tomb of a regional power during the Goguryeo kingdom based on the artifacts found at the site [1].

row.name: Sperris Quoit
row.description: Sperris Quoit is a ruined megalithic burial chamber or dolmen, and one of a type of tomb unique to West Penwith, located on a moor around 365 metres northeast of Zennor Quoit, being roughly halfway between Zennor and Amalveor, Cornwall [1]. It is the northernmost quoit in the Penwith peninsula and a Scheduled Monument [1]. Sperris Quoit is over 4000 years old, and may be older, possibly as old as 7000 years, as it has been dated variously at late- or post-Neolithic, and late Mesolithic or Neolithic [1]. It was in relatively good condition until at least the early 19th century, but there is evidence that stones have been removed since then, for local building work in the village of Zennor [1]. The site was rediscovered in 1954 by Thomas and Wakes, who excavated it in part [1]. The quoit is situated in rough moorland on the side of Zennor Hill, at about 230 metres above sea level, and is close to several rocky outcrops [1]. The capstone is missing entirely [1]. A cremation pit was discovered during the excavations, and the antechamber faces south [1].

row.name: Camel Carving Site
row.description: The Camel Carving Site is considered one of the most prominent archaeological sites of Prehistoric Arabia [1]. It dates to the Neolithic period of the Al-Jawf region in modern-day Saudi Arabia, specifically located in the eastern center of Sakaka Governorate [1]. The site "likely has the oldest known surviving large-scale animal reliefs in the world", differing in execution from the rock art common throughout Saudi Arabia [1]. The site is also considered among Saudi Arabia's oldest rock art sites, which typically feature two-dimensional carvings in both prominent and recessed styles [1].

row.name: Rough Tor
row.description: Rough Tor, or Roughtor (Cornish: Torr Garow), is a tor on Bodmin Moor, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom [1]. The site comprises the tor summit and logan stone, a Neolithic tor enclosure, many Bronze Age hut circles, and some contemporary monuments [1]. The summit of Rough Tor once had a Neolithic tor enclosure [1]. The summit is encircled by rough stone walls that align with natural stone outcroppings on the tor [1]. The walls would have originally completely encircled the tor and would have had numerous stone lined openings [1]. The Rough Tor enclosure is located in an area containing numerous upstanding monuments and other Bronze Age sites, such as Fernacre stone circle, which is only 200 metres from the site [1]. On the southern slopes of Rough Tor, there are the remains of numerous stone hut circles, set around three or four enclosures that may have held stock [1].

row.name: Julliberrie's Grave
row.description: Julliberrie's Grave, also known as The Giant's Grave or The Grave, is an unchambered long barrow located near to the village of Chilham in the south-eastern English county of Kent [1]. Probably constructed in the fourth millennium BCE, during Britain's Early Neolithic period, today it survives only in a state of ruin [1]. Julliberrie's Grave is 44 metres long, 2 metres high, and 15 metres at its widest [1]. It was originally larger, with the northern end having been destroyed [1]. A rectangular pit was dug into the western side of the barrow shortly after its completion, likely containing a ritual deposit of organic material [1]. In the Iron Age, a hearth was established in the ditch circling the barrow; in the Romano-British period, human remains and a coin hoard were buried around its perimeter [1].

row.name: Anta de Carcavelos
row.description: The Anta de Carcavelos, located close to the village of Carcavelos near the town of Lousa in the municipality of Loures in the Lisbon District of Portugal, is a stone age dolmen or megalithic monument from the Chalcolithic period [1]. The Anta was a communal grave consisting of a sepulchral chamber with a polygonal shape [1]. The remains of the tomb consist of six cretaceous limestone slabs that originated in the area, which has several sizeable limestone outcrops [1]. Hastened as a result of looting at the site, the first excavations were carried out in 1986 and continued again from 1991-1994 [1]. From the studies carried out in 1994, many bones were collected, with over 80 adult males and females believed to have been buried there [1]. Various objects were also found such as flint arrowheads, smooth and decorated bell-shaped ceramics, dishes, cylindrical idols, and objects of adornment [1]. The evaluation of items found suggested a probable initial use of the dolmen as being in the last centuries of the 4th millennium BCE, with an intensification in its use between 3000 and 2600 BCE [1].

row.name: Cloghanmore
row.description: Cloghanmore (meaning 'the great stone heap') is a megalithic court tomb in Malin More, Glencolmcille, County Donegal [1]. The monument stretches 46.3 metres in length with an oval court 16 metres long and 12 metres wide, containing twin parallel galleries divided by jamb stones [2]. Uniquely for a court tomb, two decorated orthostats bear passage tomb-style rock art with concentric circles and serpentiform designs [2] [3]. The Board of Works restored the monument in the 1880s after it was uncovered from peat [3].

row.name: Waddon Hill
row.description: Waddon Hill is a hill and the site of a short-lived Roman fort near Beaminster, in the English county of Dorset [1]. The name Waddon is from the Old English, meaning wheat hill [1]. The fort is on a narrow east-west ridge reaching a height of 210 m, with steep natural slopes to the south and west [1]. The fort was built by the Second Legion under Vespasian, but after the occupation of Dorset [1].

row.name: Tappoch Broch
row.description: Tappoch Broch, better known as Torwood Broch, is an iron-age broch located in a remote spot in dense woodland near Falkirk, Scotland [1]. Tappoch broch was first excavated in 1864 by Colonel Joseph Dundas [1]. The dry stonework is built of large, irregular stone blocks from the immediate vicinity [1]. The oval chamber measures 10.8 to 9.8 metres, is paved and has a large fire spot in the middle [1]. In the south-west of the chamber a short aisle branches off to the right and leads to an unusually well-preserved staircase in the wall [1]. Finds included saddle and rotary querns, a potential stone 'lamp' and several sherds of coarse pottery [1].

row.name: Aglaureion
row.description: The Aglaureion, or the Sanctuary of Aglauros, was an ancient sanctuary located in the Acropolis in Athens, Greece [1]. It was dedicated to Aglauros, a Greek mythological figure who was the daughter of King Cecrops and the sister of Erysichthon, Pandrosus, and Herse [1]. The sanctuary was believed to be the site where Aglauros had sacrificed herself to protect the city from invasion [1]. In 1980, during excavations of the Peripatos, archaeologists found on the eastern slope of the Acropolis an honorary stele for Aglauros, dating to the 3rd century BC [1]. It is believed the stele once stood as part of the peribolos of the Aglaureion [1].

row.name: Gudenus Cave
row.description: The Gudenus Cave is an archaeological site near the city of Krems in north-eastern Austria [1]. It is noted for its fossils and remains of Palaeolithic human settlers [1]. The Gudenus Cavern is situated 20 km northwest of the city of Krems, in the valley of the Little Krems, not far from Willendorf [1]. The cave is 22 m long with a width of 2 to 3 m and is situated 7.5 m above the level of the stream [1]. The archaeological deposit has yielded bones of numerous animals, including Woolly mammoth, Woolly rhinoceros, Aurochs, Chamois, Reindeer, and Red deer [1]. Human artifacts include numerous flint implements beginning with the Mousterian of the Middle Paleolithic, although there is no certainty as to the dating [1]. There is also an Upper Palaeolithic, Magdalenian, assemblage including an engraved reindeer bone, and a fragment of a bone flute dated to about 16,000–10,000 BCE [1].

row.name: Arsemia Ören Yeri
row.description: Arsameia on the Nymphaios is an ancient city located in Old Kâhta (Eski Kâhta) in Kâhta district, Adıyaman Province, Turkey [1]. The site is near Kâhtaçay, known in ancient times as Nymphaios [1]. Arsameia was a royal seat of the kingdom of Commagene [1]. The ancient town of Nymphaios was renamed Arsameia in the third century BCE by the Armenian king Arsames (255–225 BCE) [1]. Apart from the Hierothesion which Antiochos himself built on Nemrut Dağı, and the second one on Karakuş which his son Mithridates II built for the female members of the royal house, a third is to be found in Arsameia, the burial site and the associated cultic area for Antiochus' father Mithridates [1].

row.name: Spoonley Wood Roman Villa
row.description: Spoonley Wood Roman Villa is an ancient Roman villa located 2 km south-east of Sudeley Castle near the town of Winchcombe, in Gloucestershire, England [1]. It was a courtyard-type villa excavated in 1882 [1]. The villa lies between two streams on a north-west facing slope [1]. It measured 55 by 61 metres (180 ft × 200 ft) and was a courtyard villa [1]. The building began as a corridor villa, and was later converted by the addition of two wings extending to the north-west which were built at each end [1]. This winged villa was later turned into a courtyard villa by the addition of an enclosing wall to the north-west which connected the two wings [1]. The site was subsequently excavated by the antiquarians John Henry Middleton and William Bazeley [1]. Finds from the excavations included a silver-plated bronze bowl, a large number of 3rd- and 4th-century coins, samian ware pottery, iron knives and tools [1].

row.name: Keilor Archaeological Site
row.description: The Keilor archaeological site was among the first places to demonstrate the antiquity of Aboriginal occupation of Australia when a cranium, unearthed in 1940, was found to be nearly 15,000 years old [1] [2]. Subsequent investigations of Pleistocene alluvial terraces revealed hearths about 31,000 years BP, making Keilor one of the earliest sites of human habitation in Australia [1] [2]. Remains of megafauna suggest a possible association with Aboriginal hunting [1] [2].

row.name: Çimdin Kalesi
row.description: Cimdin Kalesi is a fortress built on a rocky hill in southeastern Turkey [1] [2]. Constructed of hard limestone with white cut stone walls and bastions, the castle was used by Byzantine, Arab, and Akkoyunlu forces [3]. The interior was filled with rubble stone, and the western entrance features large caves beneath it, surrounded by a deep defensive ditch carved directly into rock on all four sides [1] [3]. Building remains and a water well have been documented within the castle complex [1].

row.name: Solsbury Hill
row.description: Little Solsbury Hill is an Iron Age hillfort above Batheaston in Somerset, England, occupied from approximately 300 to 100 BC [1] [2]. The triangular hilltop was enclosed by a univallate rampart with dry stone walls, within which substantial timber-framed wattle-and-daub huts were built on cleared bedrock [1].

row.name: Great Yeha Temple of the Moon
row.description: The Great Yeha Temple is an ancient Sabaean tower in Tigray, Ethiopia, dating to approximately 700 BC [1] [2]. It is the oldest standing building in Ethiopia, constructed of dressed stone in a style comparable to South Arabian temples [1] [2] [3] [4]. Despite lacking radiocarbon dating, architectural similarities to ancient South Arabian structures have provided its approximate age [1]. The temple was later rededicated as a Christian church, possibly as early as the 6th century AD, which contributed to its remarkable state of preservation [1] [2].

row.name: Lancaster Roman Fort
row.description: Lancaster Roman Fort is the modern name given to a ruined former Roman fort atop Castle Hill in Lancaster in North West England [1]. The first fort at Lancaster was built out of timber, probably around 80 AD, although Roman coins have been found in Lancaster dating back to the early 60s [1]. It was likely built on this site, now known as Castle Hill, to command a crossing over the River Lune [1]. The north wall was about 187 metres long and ran east-west a short distance north of the Old Vicarage, the south side has still to be ascertained (presumed under Lancaster Castle) [1]. Later in the century the northern defences were extended by 37 metres, before it seems to have been abandoned for a period [1]. The fort was reoccupied again during the 2nd century and it was rebuilt in stone around 102 AD, with an almost 2-metre thick revetment wall built in front of the clay-and-turf rampart [1].

row.name: Castro of Monte Mozinho
row.description: The Castro of Monte Mozinho, known as the "Dead City," is a fortified settlement [1] [2]. It was founded between the late 1st century BC and early 1st century AD and occupied until the 5th century [2]. Excavations beginning in 1943 and resumed in 1974 uncovered coins, ceramics, glass, agricultural tools, and jewelry [1] [2]. An interpretive center opened in 2004 [1] [2].

row.name: Lyneham Long Barrow
row.description: Lyneham Longbarrow is a long barrow near Lyneham, Oxfordshire [1]. Just nine metres from the barrow mound stands a 1.8-metre-tall standing stone [1]. Lyneham barrow stands on a ridge overlooking valleys to the northwest and southeast [1]. The long barrow mound is 52 metres long, 19 metres wide and stands up to 1.75 metres high [1]. The stone may have been part of a facade of standing stones [1]. The barrow was excavated in 1894 [1]. The excavations located two chambers on the southeast side of the mound and at least one of these contained bone fragments, pottery and charcoal [1]. Also found were two Anglo-Saxon burials which had been cut into the top of the existing mound [1].

row.name: Bedd Taliesin
row.description: Bedd Taliesin is the legendary grave of the poet Taliesin, located in Ceredigion [1]. The Bronze Age round cairn is a listed Historic Monument [1]. It is a round-kerb cairn with a cist about 2m long [1]. The capstone has fallen; the side stone slabs are more or less in their original positions [1]. The cairn has no proven connection with the historical Taliesin, a 6th-century poet esteemed by the poets of medieval Wales as the founder of the Welsh poetic tradition [1].

row.name: Pusharo
row.description: The Petroglyphs of Pusharo constitute a unique and extensive ancient rock art archaeological site in southeastern Peru's Manú National Park, an expanse of rain forest that still contains unexplored and little known areas [1]. A smattering of adventurers began to arrive at the site in the 1950s, and in 1969 it was visited by the Peruvian physician Dr. Carlos Neuenschwander Landa [1]. In 1991 the party of North American explorer Gregory Deyermenjian arrived at Pusharo [1]. The site has since been visited and studied by rock art scholar Rainer Hostnig [1]. The site is made up of an array of deeply incised rock carvings that cover up to a height of 9 feet, a perpendicular rock face that is over 100 feet long and 75 feet high [1]. Its location is on the south shore of the Río Palatoa (designated on some maps at this location as the Porotoa, and known by others as the Palatoa Chico) [1]. The petroglyphs contain elements such as heart-shaped faces, some with double borders, spirals, zigzags, suns, "curlicue Xs" and others that defy verbal description [1].

row.name: Swastika Stone
row.description: The Swastika Stone is a stone adorned with a swastika, located on the Woodhouse Crag on the northern edge of Ilkley Moor in West Yorkshire [1]. It is the only one of its kind known in Britain [1]. The design has a double outline with four curved arms and an attached S-shape, each enclosing a so-called "cup" mark [1]. Similar cup and ring marks can be found on other stones nearby [1]. The stone has not been verifiably dated [1]. The academic consensus suggests it to have been carved sometime around the Neolithic or early Bronze Age, although Frank Elgee suggests that the design indicates a late Iron Age origin [1].

row.name: Sudheran-Jo-Thul
row.description: Sudheran-Jo-Thul is a Buddhist stupa which is situated near Tando Muhammad Khan city and Badin city in Tando Muhammad Khan District, Sindh [1]. It is located at the mound which shows the remains of a big ancient city [1]. It is located towards the south of Hyderabad city [1]. Locally, it is famous as the Tower of Sudheran [1].

row.name: Şuayb Antik Şehri
row.description: The site contains remains of residential structures built in typical Roman house styles, thought to have served as summer residences for inhabitants of the Harran Plain [1] [2]. A significant cave at the site is traditionally associated with the Prophet Shuwayb (Jethro in Biblical tradition), who according to local legend used the cave as a dwelling and place of worship [1] [2] [3] [4]. This cave continues to be venerated as a sacred site visited by pilgrims [5] [6].

row.name: Lakhmir Mound
row.description: Lakhmir Mound, locally known as Lakhmir-Ji-Mari, is a Chalcolithic archaeological site in the Naig Valley of Sindh, Pakistan, about 45 km from Sehwan Sharif [1] [2]. The mound consists of two parts: a conical hill and a lower section resembling a town [1] [3]. Archaeologist N.G. Majumdar noted Chalcolithic pottery fragments scattered across the mound and surrounding area, along with embedded stone walls from a prehistoric epoch and black-on-red pottery characteristic of the Indus Valley civilization [1].

row.name: Little Meg
row.description: Little Meg is a small circle of large kerb stones which probably surrounded a Bronze Age kerb cairn [1]. It is close to the village of Langwathby to the north-east of Penrith in the English county of Cumbria and is 650 metres north-east of the more famous stone circle of Long Meg and Her Daughters [1]. It forms part of a complex of stone circles and cairns around the Long Meg site that includes the circle at Glassonby, Old Parks, and other sites since lost [1]. Two of the stones (only one remaining) were decorated in antiquity with a series of concentric circles and a spiral [1]. When first discovered in the middle of the nineteenth century, there was a c.1.3m mound covering the stones [1]. Bones, charcoal and a 'coarse pot' were found buried in a cist at the centre of the circle [1]. Two stones found in the cist (now in Penrith Museum), have cup and ring markings [1].

row.name: Phyle Cave
row.description: The Phyle Cave is a small cave on Mount Parnes near Fyli, a suburb of Athens in Attica, Greece [1]. In ancient Greece it was the site of a sanctuary to Pan and the nymphs [1]. It is also known as Lychnospilia, meaning lamp cave, for the large number of oil lamps found in the cave [1]. It has been identified as the cave which occurs in the Dyskolos of Menander [1]. The cave was excavated in 1901 [1]. Three votive reliefs found in the cave are now on display in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens [1]. Because of its use for the veneration of Pan the cave is also called the Cave of Pan [1]. It was one of the five caves of Pan in the vicinity of ancient Athens [1].

row.name: La Marche Cave
row.description: The La Marche cave is located in the Lussac-les-Châteaux area of western France [1]. It is at the bottom of a small valley bordered by the Petit Moulin river [1]. It most likely is the result of the underground tunneling of the river [1]. The La Marche cave paintings were discovered in the caves in the Lussac-les-Châteaux area of France by Léon Péricard in November 1937 [1]. Péricard, and his partner Stephane Lwoff, studied these caves for five years and found etchings on more than 1,500 slabs [1]. In 1938, they presented their discovery to the French Prehistoric Society [1].

row.name: Stoa of Zeus
row.description: The Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios was a two-aisled stoa located in the northwest corner of the Ancient Agora of Athens [1]. It was built c. 425 BC–410 BC for religious purposes in dedication to Zeus under his epithet Eleutherios: a cult founded after the Persian War [1]. Scholars believe the building also served other civic purposes due to its central location [1]. Researchers think the structure may have been built by Mnesikles [1]. In the late first century BC a two-room annex was added, possibly for the cult of the Roman imperial family [1]. The building in all was 43.56 meters by 10.73 meters [1].

row.name: Virosidum
row.description: Virosidum was a Roman fort and settlement situated near to the modern town of Bainbridge, North Yorkshire [1]. The fort occupies a strategic position on the summit of Brough Hill, between the confluence of the River Bain and River Ure [1]. While the fort may have had an earlier phase, the visible remains date to AD 90–105 [1]. It initially had an earth and timber rampart which was rebuilt in stone around AD 190 [1]. The visible outline of the defences of the fort contains an area of 1.16 hectares (2.8 acres) [1]. The fort platform survives to a height of 3.9 m, and it is surrounded by a single ditch on the north, east and south sides, with a series of five ditches on the west [1]. The fort was first excavated by John Kirk and R. G. Collingwood in 1925–6, then by John Percival Droop for Liverpool University in 1928-9 and 1931 [1]. Five individual inscriptions have been discovered from the fort; three of these were dedicated by the Cohors VI Nerviorum, and a further two are dedicated to individual units [1].

row.name: Blowing Stone
row.description: The Blowing Stone is a perforated sarsen in Kingston Lisle, Oxfordshire, England [1]. The stone is in a garden at the foot of Blowingstone Hill just south of the Icknield Way, about 4+1⁄2 miles (7 km) west of Wantage and about 1+1⁄2 miles (2.4 km) east of White Horse Hill [1]. Blowingstone Hill is part of the escarpment of the Berkshire Downs [1]. The stone is capable of producing a booming sound if someone with the required skill blows into one of the holes the right way [1]. Legend tells that it could be heard atop White Horse Hill, where 19th-century antiquarians thought King Alfred the Great's Saxon troops had camped, and that this was how Alfred summoned them for the Battle of Ashdown against the Danes in 871 CE [1].

row.name: Ringmoor Stone Row and Cairn Circle
row.description: Ringmoor stone row and cairn circle is a prehistoric stone row and cairn circle on Ringmoor Down in Devon [1]. It is located three miles east of the A386, northeast of the village of Shaugh Prior [1]. It is three hundred metres north from Brisworthy stone circle, and is one of the archaeological sites found in the Upper Plym Valley [1]. The stone row is 356 metres long [1]. It is mainly single, but is double in parts [1]. At the southern end is a cairn circle with a diameter of 12.6 metres [1]. The central cairn is 9.5 metres in diameter and has a height of 0.4 metres [1]. A standing stone terminates the stone row at the northern end [1].

row.name: Santuário Rupestre de Panóias
row.description: The Panóias Sanctuary, also called "Fragas de Panóias", is located in Vale de Nogueiras, in the municipality of Vila Real, Portugal [1]. Its construction dates back to the end of the 2nd century - early 3rd century AD [1]. The sanctuary is an enclosure with three large rocks, where several cavities of various sizes were opened and access stairs were also built [1]. On the rock located at the entrance of the enclosure, several inscriptions were engraved - three in Latin and one in Greek, describing the ritual celebrated [1].

row.name: La Almoloya
row.description: La Almoloya is an archaeological site in Murcia, the southeast corner of the Iberian Peninsula in modern-day Spain [1]. It is a principal site of study for the Bronze Age Argaric culture that flourished from about 2200 BC to 1500 BC and controlled territory in Iberia that is equivalent in size to modern Belgium [1]. The site includes the find of what is described as an "especially rich" grave 38, which was excavated beginning in 2014 [1]. It contains the skeletal remains of a woman and a man [1]. The vast majority of the grave goods are associated with the woman; it contains numerous silver grave goods, including a diadem [1]. The couple is buried beneath the floor of a large building [1]. Radiocarbon dating suggests the burial took place at approximately 1700 BC [1]. According to Lull et al., the building above the grave may be one of the earliest Bronze Age palaces identified in Western Europe [1].

row.name: Tremeca
row.description: Tremeca is an archaeological site in Corsica [1]. The site is located in west-central Corsica, near Casaglione [1]. Tremeca was first described by the archaeologist Roger Grosjean in his 1966 overview of prehistoric Corsican sites [1]. The ancient dolmen stands in the narrowest part of a small plateau; it is approximately hemispherical in its design, supported by four rough-hewn granite blocks capped with a slab [1]. The structure of the dolmen opens toward the southeast [1]. Its design is rudimentary when compared to menhirs and other nearby structures [1]. The region has not been extensively excavated, with one of the few nearby megalithic sites being that of Monte Lazzo [1].

row.name: Whitley Castle
row.description: Whitley Castle is a large, unusually shaped Roman fort north-west of the town of Alston, Cumbria [1]. It is the highest stone-built Roman fort in Britain [1]. The castrum, which was first built by the Roman Army early in the 2nd century AD, was partly demolished and rebuilt around 200 AD [1]. It appears to have been sited to protect lead mining in the area as well as to support the border defences of Hadrian's Wall [1]. Unlike most Roman forts that have a "playing-card shape", Whitley Castle is lozenge-shaped to fit the site [1]. Numerous banks and ditches ring the stone ramparts [1]. Among finds at the fort are altars with inscriptions to Hercules by Legio VI Victrix and to Apollo by the 2nd Cohort of Nervians [1]. Other finds include a midden containing shoes; coins, fragments of Samian pottery, beads, nails, and a bronze handle shaped like a dolphin [1].

row.name: Aghios Epiktitos Vrysi
row.description: Aghios Epiktitos Vrysi, is an archaeological site in Cyprus that is located 9 km east of Kyrenia on a 9 to 10 m high cliff [1]. The site consists of at least 15 houses on an area of over 600 m2, with undercutting and subsequent demolitions that have continuously reduced the area [1]. The unusual density of the sheep and goat population as well as a considerable number of different awls and needles testify to a developed textile processing, the products of which were apparently traded and bartered outside the village [1]. Obsidian was evidently still in use, but, unlike in earlier times, it had become extremely rare in Cyprus [1]. Only one piece was found in Vrysi [1].

row.name: Great Dolmen of Comenda da Igreja
row.description: The Great Dolmen of Comenda da Igreja is a megalithic funerary site in the civil parish of Nossa Senhora do Bispo, in the municipality of Montemor-o-Novo, in the central Alentejo region of continental Portugal [1]. The articulated volumes are oriented horizontally, and covered independently in each section, with the main chamber covered by a granite slab, and the corridor by individual elements [1]. The walls of the chamber are 6 metres in height, while the corridor profile is 180 centimetres in height [1].

row.name: Sokhta Koh
row.description: Sokhta Koh (also known as Sotka Koh; lit. "burnt hill") is a Harappan site on the Makran coast, near the city of Pasni, in the Balochistan province of Pakistan [1]. It was first surveyed by American archaeologist George F. Dales in 1960, while exploring estuaries along the Makran coast [1]. Sokhta Koh is an outcrop of low hillocks in the Shadi Kaur valley, surrounded by jagged, stratified hills north of Pasni [1]. While the hillocks are about two miles in circuit, the visible remnants of the settlement, which occupy the south-eastern portion, are less than a mile around [1]. Except for a few sporadic digs, the site has not been extensively excavated [1]. The site is strewn all over by hundreds of thousands of potsherds which constitute the visible detritus of the extinct settlement [1]. Scores of open pit ovens for firing the pottery can also be discerned [1].

row.name: Llamachayuq
row.description: Llamachayuq (Quechua llama llama, -cha, -yuq suffixes, "with a little llama (or llamas)", also spelled Llamachayoq) is an archaeological complex with petroglyphs in Peru [1]. It is located in the Apurímac Region, Andahuaylas Province, San Jerónimo District [1]. The site with images of llamas, vicuñas, felines, people and the sun lies near Lliwpa Pukyu (Lliupapuquio) at a height of 3,449 metres (11,316 ft) [1].

row.name: Jajce Mithraeum
row.description: The Jajce Mithraeum, or Jajački Mithraeum is a mithraeum, or temple of Mithraism [1]. The temple dates back to the early 4th century, although it could be as ancient as the 2nd century with repairs undertaken during the early 4th century [1]. This particular Mithraeum is one of the best-preserved sites in Europe [1]. The Jajce site is a typical spelaea [1]. The remains of the Mithraeum in Jajce were discovered accidentally during excavation for the construction of a private house in 1931 [1]. The site was purchased by the Society for the Preservation of Antiquities in Jajce and soon after a protective stone and mortar structure was constructed under the supervision of engineer F. Steiner [1].

row.name: Tenayuca
row.description: Tenayuca is a pre-Columbian Mesoamerican archaeological site in the Valley of Mexico [1]. In the Postclassic period of Mesoamerican chronology, Tenayuca was a settlement on the former shoreline of the western arm of Lake Texcoco [1]. It was located approximately 10 kilometres to the northwest of Tenochtitlan [1]. Aztec temple architecture primarily developed at Tenayuca, which has the earliest example yet found of the typical Aztec double pyramid, which consists of joined pyramidal bases supporting two temples [1]. The temple of Tenayuca is better preserved than the similar temple of Tlatelolco and its wall of serpents remains mostly intact on three sides of the base of the pyramid [1]. The site consists of a massive truncated temple platform with a double stairway rising on the western side to where the twin temples of Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli once stood [1]. Some of the temple steps are carved with year-glyphs such as knives, circles and shields [1]. In the case of Tenayuca, the size of the building increased through six phases of construction but the basic form remained unchanged [1].

row.name: Cabezo Juré
row.description: Cabezo Juré is an archaeological site located in Alosno, Andalusia from the 3rd millennium BC [1]. The archaeological excavations have recently revealed the vestiges of an ancient community of workers specialized in the metallurgy of copper [1]. Calibrated radiocarbon age revealed it was active between 2873 and 2274 BC [1].

row.name: Rhodes Footbridge
row.description: The Rhodes Footbridge is an ancient Greek arch bridge in the city of Rhodes, Greece [1]. Dating to the 4th century BC or early Hellenistic period, the modest structure represents the oldest known Greek bridge with a voussoir arch [1]. The Rhodes Footbridge was unearthed in 1966−67 close to the eastern harbour of the city of Rhodes, the Akandia Bay [1]. There, an artificial channel of 2.15 m depth ran parallel to the ancient city walls, separated by an 11 m wide street running in between [1]. The sidewalls of the conduit were made of at least four layers of poros stone blocks, the same material also employed for the arch [1]. Nearly at its midpoint, the canal is crossed by an 8 m broad arch of wedge-shaped stones which served as a footbridge [1]. The curved opening has a single span of 2.8 m, identical to the width of the canal [1]. Its surprisingly low rise, in the order of 1 to 3−4, gives it the appearance of a segmental or even multi-centered arch, of which it is the only known example in Greek architecture [1].

row.name: Thermes Romains en Ruine-Roman Baths
row.description: The Roman Baths of Beirut date to the Roman imperial period when Berytus had four major bath complexes [1] [2]. Located in downtown Beirut between Banks Street and Capuchin Street, the baths were discovered in 1968 and feature a hypocaust underfloor heating system with terracotta disk pillars [1]. All of Berytus' baths were destroyed by the catastrophic earthquake of 551 AD [1] [2]. One of the preserved bath ruins is occasionally used as an artistic performance and concert space [1].

row.name: Balberta
row.description: Balberta is a major Mesoamerican archaeological site on the Pacific coastal plain of southern Guatemala, belonging to the Maya civilization [1]. It has been dated to the Early Classic period and is the only known major site on the Guatemalan Pacific coastal plain to have exposed Early Classic architecture that has not been buried under posterior Late Classic construction [1]. Balberta first appears to have been occupied in the Late Preclassic period, when it was a small site of minor importance [1]. After a period of rapid growth it became one of the largest Early Classic sites on the Guatemalan Pacific coast and reached the height of its power between AD 200 and AD 400 [1]. It traded with the distant metropolis of Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico [1]. At its height Balberta demonstrated true state-level political organisation and dominated a wide swathe of the Guatemalan coast [1]. Balberta was suddenly abandoned around AD 400 [1]. The site core consists of 22 structures occupying an area of 18 hectares [1].

row.name: Withypool Stone Circle
row.description: Withypool Stone Circle, also known as Withypool Hill Stone Circle, is a stone circle located on the Exmoor moorland, near the village of Withypool in the southwestern English county of Somerset [1]. The ring is part of a tradition of stone circle construction that spread throughout much of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany during the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age [1]. The Withypool ring is located on the south-western slope of Withypool Hill, on an area of heathland [1]. It is about 36.4 metres in diameter [1]. Around thirty small gritstones remain, although there may originally have been around 100; there are conspicuous gaps on the northern and western sides of the monument [1]. The site was rediscovered in 1898 and surveyed by the archaeologist Harold St George Gray in 1905 [1]. The site is 381 metres above sea level [1].

row.name: Rocha dos Namorados
row.description: The Rocha dos Namorados (Lovers’ Rock) is a large upright granite stone located in the parish of Corval, municipality of Reguengos de Monsaraz, in the Évora District of the Alentejo region of Portugal [1]. It is sometimes considered to be a menhir or standing stone but there is no evidence of it having been placed at the site and it seems to be a natural outcrop, although it does have some dimpled, megalithic engravings, as well as a cross, which is believed to have been carved in order to Christianise what was an ancient ritual [1]. It is considered a rare example of the veneration of stones associated with a secular, pagan fertility rite that has continued to the present [1]. The stone is more than two meters high, and has a shape similar to that of a mushroom, with the top having a circumference of about 7 meters [1]. The fertility rite involves girls of marriageable age consulting the rock to find out how long before they get married [1].

row.name: Holm of Papa Chambered Cairn
row.description: The Holm of Papa is a very small uninhabited island in the Orkney Islands [1]. The main sight on the small island is the Southcairn, a 20 metre long chambered cairn dating from approx. 3000 BC on whose stones one can find ancient carvings [1]. The long, stalled cairn, built of local stone, was once a communal burial place for the bones of an ancient community [1]. It is protected by a modern roof and entered by a trapdoor from above [1]. It is possible that the inhabitants of the Knap of Howar buried their dead here [1]. There are three ancient chambered cairns on the holm [1].

row.name: Nemean Baths
row.description: The Nemean baths are an athletic bathing house at the Panhellenic sanctuary of Nemea in the Argolis [1]. The baths are located in the southernmost part of the Hellenistic complex [1]. They are directly west of the similarly dated Xenon, which served as athletes' lodging [1]. Though the sanctuary had existed since the Archaic period, the baths are thought to have been built in the 4th century BC [1]. The bath itself is divided between a west wing with a series of basins and an east wing with an open bath [1]. Along with the Xenon, the bath served as amenities to athletes during the Nemean Games [1]. The east wing's circular immersion bath or 'plunge bath' is remarkable as it is one of only four in Greece [1]. Early Christians turned the temple of Zeus into a Basilica in the 5th century AD and used the open chamber of the bath house as a repository for the dead; thus far, three burials have been found [1].

row.name: Grey Wethers
row.description: Grey Wethers consists of a pair of prehistoric stone circles, situated on grassy plateau to the north of Postbridge, Dartmoor [1]. The circles are each approximately 33 m in diameter, and less than five metres apart [1]. Their centre points are aligned almost exactly north to south [1]. The northern circle has 20 stones remaining, while the southern has 29 – all of a relatively consistent size, mostly between 1.2 and 1.4 m in height [1]. An excavation was carried out in 1898 and a number of charcoal fragments were discovered within the circles [1]. The circles were restored and many fallen stones re-erected in 1909 [1].

row.name: Utroba Cave
row.description: The Utroba Cave, also known as Womb Cave, is an ancient cave sanctuary in Kardzhali Province [1]. Located in the Eastern Rhodope Mountains near the Ilinitsa village, the cave resembles a human vulva and dates to the Thracian period [1]. Historians believe that it was once used as a fertility shrine [1]. The cave is located 20 kilometers from the city of Kardzhali near the village of Ilinitsa and it dates to 480 BC [1]. The inside of the cave resembles a uterus [1]. Researchers believe that the entrance to the cave was a slit, which was then widened by humans [1]. The entrance to the cave is 3 metres tall and 2.50 m wide and inside the cave there is a 1.3 m-tall altar which has been carved [1].

row.name: Roman Remains under Alfonso X Street
row.description: The Roman remains under Alfonso X street, generally called "the chambers of Hacienda", are located in the city of Toledo, in Castilla-La Mancha, Spain [1]. The remains are chambers that supplied water to a thermal bath dated from around 1st century AD [1]. There is one large arched central gallery, entered through three parallel arched galleries, that reside beneath the hypocaust of the thermal baths at Plaza de Amador de los Ríos [1]. They were hidden until 1628 when construction began on the Society of Jesus building, which was recorded by Julio Porres [1]. They were rediscovered in 1918 [1].

row.name: Tolvan Holed Stone
row.description: The Tolvan holed stone is a large triangular-shaped standing stone [1]. It measures 2.3 m high, 2.3 m wide at the base, and is 0.3 m thick [1]. Near the base of the monument is a circular hole, approximately 43 cm in diameter [1]. The standing stone is located about 800 m north of the village of Gweek in Cornwall, England, behind the farmhouse at Tolvan Cross [1]. The Tolvan stone is the largest holed stone in Cornwall [1]. "Tolvan" originated from the term, toll-ven meaning holed stone in Cornish [1]. The Tolvan holed stone is mentioned in historical records in Cornwall in 1649, and is referred to as the "Main-toll great stone" [1].

row.name: Aigeira
row.description: The archaeological site of ancient Aigeira is located approximately 6 km from the modern town [1]. It is an important site for the Mycenaean and later periods, with particularly extensive remains from the Hellenistic period [1]. Settlement at Aigeira is known from the Middle Neolithic and Final Neolithic, beginning around 5500 BCE [1]. The first settlement was situated on the acropolis, and has furnished evidence of pottery, including vessels likely used in the production of cheese [1]. Some evidence of Neolithic settlement has been found on a lower plateau, approximately 150m to the east of the acropolis [1]. Like many Aegean sites, Aigeira was abandoned at the end of the Bronze Age, following the destruction of the site at the end of LH IIIC Middle [1]. Occupation began again in the second half of the 8th century BCE, likely associated with the sanctuary at the site [1]. Some partial fortifications are known from the Archaic period, covering an area of around 3.5 hectares [1].

row.name: Fraubillen Cross
row.description: The Fraubillen cross (German: Fraubillenkreuz) is a menhir, which has been resculpted into a cross [1]. It stands by a wayside on the Ferschweiler Plateau in the Eifel mountains in Germany, between Ferschweiler, Schankweiler, Nusbaum-Rohrbach and Bollendorf [1]. According to tradition, the celebrated missionary in the Eifel region, Willibrord refashioned the roughly 5,000-year-old menhir by hand into the shape of a cross as a Christian monument [1]. Two niches for figures have been chiselled into the rock, each surrounded by holes [1]. Today, the cross is about 3.5 metres high [1].

row.name: Qollmay
row.description: Qollmay is 4 km North-West (about a 25-minute drive on dirt road) of Chinchaypujio [1]. First excavated by Max Uhle in 1905 and registered by Ken Heffernan in 1986, it has been classified in 6 sectors and has about a dozen foundations, half a dozen well preserved walls and one well preserved walled-off natural cavern with Inca-style stonework inside, located within sector 1 [1]. This cavernous building is thought to be the most important one in the whole site [1]. Adjacent to it is a rock formation reminiscent of a birth canal, speculated to be the site of fertility rituals [1]. The site is embedded within Inca-made, rectangular terraces, now overgrown with grass [1].

row.name: Cetina
row.description: The Cetina Valley and the narrow passage at Klis have always functioned as a principal trade route between the Croatian coast and hinterland [1]. The earliest evidence for agricultural activity is from the Early Neolithic in the upper part of the valley [1]. In the Early Bronze Age the Cetina culture, a geographically pervasive group with contacts throughout the Adriatic basin, became dominant [1]. Extensive mound fields are recorded on the lower valley slopes at several locations around Cetina, Vrlika and Bajagić [1].

row.name: Bruniquel Cave
row.description: Bruniquel Cave is an archeological site near Bruniquel, in an area which has many paleolithic sites, east of Montauban in southwestern France [1]. Annular (ring) and accumulation (pile) structures made of broken stalagmites have been found 336 metres from the cave entrance [1]. Traces of fire were also found [1]. In a letter to Nature reporting the discovery in 2016, Jacques Jaubert and his co-authors state the structures are of anthropogenic origin, and as early Neanderthals were the only humans in the area at that time, they must have been the builders [1]. Bruniquel Cave was closed naturally during the Pleistocene [1]. The artificial ring structures made of broken stalagmites now have been dated by uranium series dating as 176.5 thousand years old [1]. Approximately 400 stalagmite pieces were used in the construction of the structure, with a total length of 112.4 metres and weight of approximately 2.2 tons [1].

row.name: Yarim Tepe
row.description: Yarim Tepe is an archaeological site of an early farming settlement that goes back to about 6000 BC [1]. It is located in the Sinjar valley some 7km southwest from the town of Tal Afar in northern Iraq [1]. The site consists of several hills reflecting the development of the Hassuna culture, and then of the Halaf and Ubaid cultures [1]. The settlement was investigated between 1969 and 1976, and later by the Soviet archaeological expedition under the leadership of Rauf Munchaev and Nikolai Merpert [1]. Yarim Tepe II is a settlement of the Halafian culture, belonging to the fifth millennium BC [1]. Metal was already quite common at Yarim Tepe; as many as 21 examples of worked copper or copper ore were found in the lower levels of the settlement [1].

row.name: The Gop
row.description: The Gop (Welsh: Coparleni, also known as Gop Cairn or Gop-y-Goleuni) is a Neolithic monument lying within the Clwydian Range, northwest of Trelawnyd, in Flintshire, Wales [1]. Sitting on top of Gop Hill, a natural outcrop of Carboniferous Limestone, the cairn mound is 75-80m in diameter and 12m high [1].

row.name: Consuegra Dam
row.description: The Consuegra Dam is a ruined Roman buttress dam in Toledo province, Castilla–La Mancha [1]. The dam dates to the 3rd or 4th century AD [1]. It is on the River Amarguillo upstream from Consuegra [1]. Although less than 5 metres high, the dam was remarkably long, over 600 metres [1]. The reservoir seems to have had a dual function of supplying water to Consuegra and irrigating farmland [1].

row.name: Lebak Cibedug Temple
row.description: Lebak Cibedug temple, is a terraced pyramid shaped sacred megalithic site on the bank of Cibedug river near Citorek village in Banten Province at the west end of the island of Java [1]. The site is located on the slope of Pasir Manggu hill [1]. Cibedug pyramid has nine terraces with menhirs and altars on them [1]. Square shaped terraces were constructed with oval-shaped andesite stones [1]. Lebak Cibedug monument design is older than the temples of Bali [1].

row.name: Pirak
row.description: Pirak is an archaeological site belonging to the Indus Valley civilization located in Balochistan [1]. It is 20 km south of Sibi east of the Nari River [1]. The site of Pirak was first reported by Robert Raikes in 1963 [1]. It was excavated, between 1968 and 1974, before the well known sites of Mehrgarh or Nausharo by the French archaeological mission team led by Jean Marie Casal [1]. According to the excavator, this site was occupied from c.1800 BCE to 800 BCE [1]. The site has some very early ironwork and iron artefacts [1]. The excavator records three phases of unbroken occupation in Safi pirak [1]. The earliest indubitable evidence of domestic horse comes from Safi Pirak, during period I (c.1700 BC) [1].

row.name: Branodunum
row.description: Branodunum was an ancient Roman fort to the east of the modern English village of Brancaster in Norfolk [1]. The fort, built in the 230s, became later part of the eleven forts along the south and east coasts of England [1]. It was built to guard the Wash approaches and is of a typical rectangular castrum layout [1]. According to the 4th-century document Notitia Dignitatum, the fort was garrisoned by the Equites Dalmatae Brandodunenses, although a tile found on the site stamped Cohors I Aquitanorum suggests that its original garrison was the "First cohort from Aquitania" [1]. There is possible evidence of later Anglo-Saxon use of the site [1]. In Roman times, the fort's northern wall lay directly on the seashore, which served as a harbour [1]. Since then, the shoreline has accreted, and the fort now lies inland of salt marshes [1]. The fort was of a rectangular shape with rounded corners, with a 10 ft wide wall with internal turrets at the corners and backed by an earthen rampart, which increased the wall's strength and gave easy access to the battlements [1].

row.name: Castle Goff
row.description: Castle Goff is an enclosure about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) south-west of Camelford, in Cornwall [1]. It is a scheduled monument [1]. Castle Goff is considered to be a "round": these are small circular embanked enclosures, with one entrance; they date from the late Iron Age to the early post-Roman period [1]. They are most common in Cornwall [1]. It is situated on the southern edge of a ridge between two tributaries of the River Allen [1]. Its diameter is about 60 metres (66 yd) [1]. The rampart is 1.8 metres (5.9 ft) above the interior, and 3.5 metres (11 ft) above the external ditch, which is about 8 metres (26 ft) wide and 0.8 metres (2.6 ft) deep [1]. From the original western entrance, which is now blocked, there is a causeway to an annexe to the west [1].

row.name: Lohra Megalithic Tomb
row.description: The Lohra tomb was a megalithic monument outside Lohra near Marburg in north central Hesse, Germany [1]. It is one of the lesser known among its type in Central Europe [1]. It dates to the Late Neolithic, probably just after 3000 BC [1]. It belongs to the gallery graves of the Wartberg culture, but is unique among them because of its rich ceramic assemblage [1]. The tomb was discovered accidentally in 1931 by the farmer Jakob Elmshäuser who encountered an obstacle when ploughing a field [1]. The tomb consisted of a large main chamber and a small open antechamber [1]. In contrast to the finds from the well-known tombs at Züschen or Altendorf, the dead at Lohra had been cremated [1]. 20 vessels that had been placed on the chamber floor and later covered in human ashes were almost fully preserved [1].

row.name: Sweet Track
row.description: The Sweet Track is an ancient trackway, or causeway, in the Somerset Levels, England, named after its finder, Ray Sweet [1]. The Sweet Track was predominantly built along the course of an earlier structure, the Post Track [1]. The track extended across the now largely drained marsh between what was then an island at Westhay and a ridge of high ground at Shapwick, a distance close to 1,800 metres or around 1.1 mi [1]. Various artifacts and prehistoric finds, including a jadeitite ceremonial axe head, have been found in the peat bogs along its length [1]. The track was used for a period of only around ten years and was then abandoned, probably due to rising water levels [1]. The track was discovered in 1970 during peat excavations and is named after its finder, Ray Sweet [1]. Built in 3807 or 3806 BC, the track was a walkway consisting mainly of planks of oak laid end-to-end, supported by crossed pegs of ash, oak, and lime, driven into the underlying peat [1].

row.name: Bouldnor Cliff
row.description: Bouldnor Cliff is a submerged prehistoric settlement site in the Solent [1]. The site dates from the Mesolithic era and is in approximately 11 metres of water just offshore of the village of Bouldnor on the Isle of Wight in the United Kingdom [1]. Several years of fieldwork have revealed that Bouldnor was a settlement site about 8,000 years ago, at a time when lower sea levels meant that the Solent was just a river valley [1]. As sea levels rose, the Solent eventually flooded and the settlement area was swamped [1]. The rising waters deposited silt and mud onto the original land surface, covering and preserving it [1]. Archaeologists have discovered large quantities of burnt flints, mounds of timbers and pits dug into the ground [1]. Wood from this era does not normally preserve well in land environments, so the quantity of wood found at Bouldnor makes the site of international importance [1].

row.name: Gobustan Rock Art
row.description: The Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape is a historic site in Azerbaijan, comprising a large collection of petroglyphs that reflect the flora, fauna, hunting practices, social structures, and cultural expressions of human societies from prehistoric to medieval times [1]. These engravings provide detailed depictions of anthropomorphic figures, such as lance-bearers and ritualistic dance scenes, as well as various animal species, bullfighting events, camel caravans, and celestial symbols such as the sun and other stars [1]. The Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape reflects the history of human development in Eurasia from the Upper Paleolithic era through the Middle Ages [1]. It is situated at the southeastern end of the Greater Caucasus ridge, approximately 70 km southwest of central Baku, and covers an area of 537 hectares [1]. The rock art was accidentally discovered by quarry workers in the 1930s [1].
