row.old_value: 5th-4th millennium BC Neolithic cairn in the Clwydian Range, Flintshire — the second-largest Neolithic mound in Britain after Silbury Hill.
row.new_value: Sitting on top of Gop Hill, a natural outcrop of Carboniferous Limestone, the cairn mound is 75-80m in diameter and 12m high.

row.old_value: The largest Roman mosaic yet found in Somerset came from an eight-room villa. A mechanical digger in 2001 struck coloured stone cubes just centimetres below a farmer's field, exposing the floor.
A double-banked Iron Age fort covering 3.4 hectares, dating to around 50 BC. Its multivallate design suggests a community expecting serious threats.
An 8 km sandstone ridge dotted with Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments spanning 2,000+ years. A massive erratic boulder called Arthur's Stone sits near the summit.
row.new_value: Just north of the ridge summit of Cefn Bryn, there is a Neolithic burial ground, known as "Arthur's Stone".

row.old_value: A Roman-era castle built along the Via Egnatia, with walls once 12 metres high. The last resident was Demir Pasha during the Ottoman period.
row.new_value: The foundations of the castle are thought to date from the Roman period, the time of the construction of the Via Egnatia.

row.old_value: Ruined quoit in West Penwith, dated variously to the Late or Post-Neolithic and as far back as 5000 BC. Two uprights and a displaced capstone survive on a moor near Zennor.
row.new_value: The quoit is situated in rough moorland on the side of Zennor Hill, at about 230 metres above sea level, and is close to several rocky outcrops.

row.old_value: Near Chilham in Kent, this unchambered long barrow from the fourth millennium BC survives in ruin. Built by early farming communities shortly after pastoralism arrived from continental Europe.
Woodland broch near Falkirk, first studied in 1864 by Colonel Dundas and later laser-scanned after conservation work cleared the scrub. The circular chamber measured about 9 m across.
row.new_value: Tappoch Broch, better known as Torwood Broch, is an iron-age broch located in a remote spot in dense woodland near Falkirk.

row.old_value: A skull unearthed in 1940 proved nearly 15,000 years old; later digs found hearths from 29,000 BC. Keilor is one of the earliest habitation sites on the continent; megafauna remains suggest hunting.
Deep in Manú National Park, a government permit is required to enter. Over 30 metres of perpendicular cliff face holds deeply incised carvings reaching 2.7 metres high — purpose still debated.
row.new_value: The site is made up of an array of deeply incised rock carvings that cover up to a height of 9 feet, a perpendicular rock face that is over 100 feet long and 75 feet high.

row.old_value: A conical mound from around 3000 BC with a lower section that resembles a planned town. It dates to the same era as the great Indus Valley cities.
~3000 BC dolmen above Casaglione village in Corsica, with a distinctive semicircular capstone. One of the island's inland megalithic monuments, raised by communities known only through their stones.
A Neolithic clifftop settlement from 4400-3800 BC with at least 15 houses on 600 square metres. Residents carved tunnels through the cliff to connect their homes.
row.new_value: The site consists of at least 15 houses on an area of over 600 m2, with undercutting and subsequent demolitions that have continuously reduced the area.

row.old_value: A megalithic tomb from the 4th–3rd millennium BC built by semi-nomadic communities of the ancient Alentejo region. It stands isolated in an area of forested brush.
row.new_value: The walls of the chamber are 6 metres in height, while the corridor profile is 180 centimetres in height.

row.old_value: 20-metre chambered cairn on a tiny uninhabited Orkney island, built around 3000 BC. Ancient carvings mark its stones — accessible only from Papa Westray, less than 100 metres away.
row.new_value: The main sight on the small island is the Southcairn, a 20 metre long chambered cairn dating from approx. 3000 BC on whose stones one can find ancient carvings.

row.old_value: A cave carved to resemble a human womb, used as a Thracian fertility shrine from around 480 BC. The interior narrows into a symbolic birth canal.
A settlement continuously inhabited since 3100 BC. Homer mentioned it in the Iliad, and its acropolis ruins span Bronze Age through Roman layers.
Ring structures made of broken stalagmites found 336 metres deep in this cave date to 176,000 years ago. They are the oldest known constructions by Neanderthals.
row.new_value: The artificial ring structures made of broken stalagmites now have been dated by uranium series dating as 176.5 thousand years old.

row.old_value: A small Iron Age "round" -- a circular embanked enclosure 60 metres across with a single entrance. These enclosures are found almost exclusively in one region.
row.new_value: Castle Goff is considered to be a "round": these are small circular embanked enclosures, with one entrance; they date from the late Iron Age to the early post-Roman period.

row.old_value: Rock carvings spanning 20,000 years — from Upper Paleolithic hunting scenes to medieval camel caravans. A visual timeline of human culture etched into stone.
row.new_value: The Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape reflects the history of human development in Eurasia from the Upper Paleolithic era through the Middle Ages.

row.old_value: 200-metre hilltop near Yatton in North Somerset shared by Bronze Age barrows, a scheduled Iron Age fort, and a Roman villa -- three distinct periods of occupation layered on one summit.
row.new_value: The hill fort was refortified around 400, after the urban collapse associated with the withdrawal of Rome, and occupation extended into the sub-Roman period.

row.old_value: A hillfort so large it is considered one of the biggest Iron Age enclosures in its region. Its stone-walled defenses stretch along the summit at 350 meters elevation.
row.new_value: Y Garn Goch is a hill in the Brecon Beacons National Park in the east of Carmarthenshire.

row.old_value: A Paleolithic cave system with over 500 art figures, 40 hand stencils, and 4,000 fossils. A sealed chamber preserves a campsite floor untouched for 16,000 years.
row.new_value: The cave complex is noted for one of the best preserved floors from the Paleolithic containing more than 4,000 fossils and more than 500 graphical units.

row.old_value: 1000–1500 AD. Petroglyphs at 3,449 m carve llamas, vicuñas, felines, people, and the sun into Andean rock — a vivid record of life and belief in the high Apurímac mountains.
row.new_value: The site with images of llamas, vicuñas, felines, people and the sun lies near Lliwpa Pukyu at a height of 3,449 metres.

row.old_value: A multivallate hillfort on a triangular promontory, enclosed by a ditch 4 metres wide. Two spurs of a river valley provided natural defences on most sides.
row.new_value: Bury Camp, an Iron Age hillfort on a triangular promontory of Colerne Down, was built about 350 BC, yet the Neolithic and Mesolithic flint tools found there point to a much earlier use.

row.old_value: The largest surviving fogou in Cornwall — an underground dry-stone passage from the Iron Age whose original purpose remains a mystery. Storage, shelter, or ritual? Nobody knows.
row.new_value: A long narrow tunnel roofed and walled in stone leads to three chambers: Halliggye Fogou, the largest and best-preserved of several mysterious tunnels linked to Cornish Iron Age settlements.

row.old_value: Crowning the second-highest peak in the Clwydian Range at 511 metres, this hillfort covers 10 hectares. Offa's Dyke Path passes around its western slopes.
row.new_value: On the peak of Foel Fenlli, ramparts enclose a hillfort with hut platforms and a spring. Legend says king Benlli probably lived here, till fire from heaven consumed him and his castle.

row.old_value: A Baekje kingdom earthen fortification with walls 2.7 km long and up to 7 metres high. It defended the ancient capital during a period of constant warfare between three rival kingdoms.
row.new_value: The Baekje walls of Mongchontoseong Earthen Fortification are estimated at about 2.7 km long and approximately 6 to 7 m high, with a palisade on top and a moat around the base.

row.old_value: The quoit is situated in rough moorland on the side of Zennor Hill, at about 230 metres above sea level, and is close to several rocky outcrops.
row.new_value: On the rough moorland of Zennor Hill lies Sperris Quoit, a ruined burial chamber over 4000 years old. Its capstone is missing entirely; excavation uncovered a cremation pit.

row.old_value: Six cretaceous limestone slabs still upright from the 4th–3rd millennium BC — a communal grave near Loures whose builders dragged multi-tonne stone across the landscape without metal tools.
row.new_value: Six limestone slabs remain of the Anta de Carcavelos, a Chalcolithic communal grave. Over 80 adults are believed buried here, and flint arrowheads and cylindrical idols were found.

row.old_value: A Roman courtyard villa with a mosaic still viewable under a corrugated roof. Finds include Samian Ware pottery and hundreds of Roman coins.
row.new_value: Between two streams near Winchcombe, Spoonley Wood Roman Villa grew from a corridor villa into a courtyard villa. Its finds: a silver-plated bronze bowl and many 3rd- and 4th-century coins.

row.old_value: A 4th-century BC bathing house for athletes at the sanctuary of Nemea. It sat beside the athletes' lodging and served competitors in the Panhellenic Games.
row.new_value: Thought to date to the 4th century BC, the Nemean Baths served athletes of the Nemean Games. Their circular plunge bath is one of only four in Greece; three burials were later found here.

row.old_value: A pair of stone circles on Dartmoor, each 33 metres across and less than 5 metres apart, aligned almost exactly north to south. The name means "grey sheep" — the stones' silhouette.
row.new_value: North of Postbridge on Dartmoor stand the Grey Wethers: two stone circles, each approximately 33 m across and less than five metres apart, aligned almost exactly north to south.

row.old_value: Sitting on top of Gop Hill, a natural outcrop of Carboniferous Limestone, the cairn mound is 75-80m in diameter and 12m high.
row.new_value: Crowning Gop Hill, an outcrop of Carboniferous Limestone in the Clwydian Range of Flintshire, The Gop is a Neolithic cairn mound 75-80m in diameter and 12m high.

row.old_value: A Roman fort whose Celtic name may mean "fort of the raven," built in the 230s to guard the Wash. It became part of the Saxon Shore defence system against raiders.
row.new_value: In Roman times the northern wall of Branodunum stood on the seashore, which served as a harbour. Now the fort, built in the 230s to guard the Wash approaches, lies inland of salt marshes.

row.old_value: Two standing stones near the Hurlers stone circles, each about 2 m high. Legend says they were men turned to stone for playing music on the Sabbath.
row.new_value: On Bodmin Moor stand The Pipers, two stones approximately 2 metres high. Folklore makes them musicians, playing for three circles of dancers turned to stone for revelling on a holy day.

row.old_value: Y Garn Goch is a hill in the Brecon Beacons National Park in the east of Carmarthenshire.
row.new_value: On the hill of Y Garn Goch, the red cairn, lie two impressive Iron Age hillforts, the big fort and the little fort: in the established view, together the largest in southern Wales.

row.old_value: The cave complex is noted for one of the best preserved floors from the Paleolithic containing more than 4,000 fossils and more than 500 graphical units.
row.new_value: At La Garma Cave Complex, a rockslide sealed the original entrance about 16,000 years ago, keeping a Paleolithic floor pristine: more than 4,000 fossils, and an ibex carved on a bovine rib.

row.old_value: A passage grave built with heavy boulders and capstones, assigned to the Funnelbeaker culture. The cemetery also contains unchambered long barrows and other tumuli.
row.new_value: In Western Pomerania, the Borkowo Megalithic Cemetery gathers long barrows and a passage grave of heavy boulders and capstones, where excavators found a cremation and a few pottery sherds.

row.old_value: 1st-or-2nd-century BC fort in Worcestershire. The name "Berry" derives from burgh — a defensive position; local tradition also calls it "Danes Bury" after a Norse raiding legend.
row.new_value: On the outskirts of Birmingham, the Iron Age hill fort of Berry Mound kept a V-shaped ditch 22 ft wide to the south. A third line of ramparts, seen in the 19th century, has left no traces.

row.old_value: A Roman fort founded around 80 AD, rebuilt multiple times over four centuries. Its garrison helped defend the northwest coast against Irish Sea raiders.
row.new_value: Atop Castle Hill, Lancaster Roman Fort began in timber, probably around 80 AD, likely to command a crossing of the River Lune. Its south side is presumed to lie under Lancaster Castle.

row.old_value: Round Bronze Age cairn in Ceredigion, about 2 metres long, with its capstone fallen and side slabs still in position. The grave bears no proven connection to the 6th-century poet Taliesin.
row.new_value: Legend calls Bedd Taliesin the grave of the poet Taliesin, though no connection is proven: a Bronze Age cairn in Ceredigion with a cist about 2m long, its capstone fallen.

row.old_value: A small cave sacred to Pan and the nymphs, known as "Lamp Cave" for the many oil lamps found inside. It has been identified as the setting for a comedy by Menander.
row.new_value: On Mount Parnes, the small Phyle Cave once held a sanctuary to Pan and the nymphs. So many oil lamps were found inside that it is also called Lychnospilia, the lamp cave.

row.old_value: A Roman fort controlling a Pennine pass between Stainmore and the Aire gap. Its hilltop position provided unobstructed views across the entire valley.
row.new_value: On the summit of Brough Hill, where the Bain meets the Ure, the Roman fort of Virosidum traded its earth and timber rampart for stone around AD 190. Five ditches guard its west.

row.old_value: A 2nd-century AD Roman sanctuary with cavities of various sizes carved into three large cliffs. Steps cut into the rock lead to ritual platforms.
row.new_value: Santuário Rupestre de Panóias is an enclosure of three large rocks with cavities opened in them and stairs built. On the entrance rock, Latin and Greek inscriptions describe the ritual.

row.old_value: A site of the El Argar culture (2200-1500 BC), which controlled territory the size of Belgium. An exceptionally rich female burial hints at women holding power.
row.new_value: At La Almoloya, a woman and a man lie beneath the floor of a large building, their grave holding numerous silver goods including a diadem. Radiocarbon dating suggests approximately 1700 BC.

row.old_value: Built 200–400 AD on the Pacific coastal plain, Balberta is the only known Early Classic Maya site there with exposed architecture not buried by later construction.
row.new_value: On the Pacific coastal plain, Balberta grew into a Maya power that traded with distant Teotihuacan, peaked between AD 200 and AD 400, and was then suddenly abandoned around AD 400.

row.old_value: A stone circle on Exmoor moorland, part of a Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age tradition. The purpose of these rings is unknown, though ritual gathering is widely suspected.
row.new_value: On Exmoor heathland, the Withypool Stone Circle keeps around thirty small gritstones in a ring about 36.4 metres across, where there may once have been around 100. Gaps open north and west.
In the Eastern Rhodope Mountains, the Utroba Cave resembles a human vulva, its inside a uterus. A carved altar stands within; historians believe it was once used as a fertility shrine.

row.old_value: A roughly 5,000-year-old menhir resculpted into a Christian cross, reportedly by the missionary Willibrord. Niches for saint figures were chiselled into the ancient stone.
row.new_value: By a wayside on the Ferschweiler Plateau stands the Fraubillen Cross, a roughly 5,000-year-old menhir that, according to tradition, the missionary Willibrord reshaped by hand into a cross.

row.old_value: Timber causeway built in 3807 BC across the Somerset Levels—dendrochronology dated it to the exact year. The second-oldest timber trackway of its type found in the islands.
row.new_value: Oak planks laid end-to-end on crossed pegs of ash, oak and lime: the Sweet Track, built in 3807 or 3806 BC across a Somerset marsh, was used for only around ten years, then abandoned.

row.old_value: The Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape reflects the history of human development in Eurasia from the Upper Paleolithic era through the Middle Ages.
row.new_value: Lance-bearers, ritual dances, camel caravans, the sun and other stars: quarry workers stumbled on the Gobustan Rock Art in the 1930s, engravings from prehistoric to medieval times.

row.old_value: An island inhabited since 7000 BC, used as a Viking-era meeting place due to its central location. Its name's etymology is completely unknown.
row.new_value: In the Kattegat, Samsø was cut at its narrowest place by a canal about 500 m long, dug and clad with wooden linings in the years 726–729 AD. In the Viking Age it became a meeting place.

row.old_value: The foundations of the castle are thought to date from the Roman period, the time of the construction of the Via Egnatia.
row.new_value: From Peqin Castle, tunnels led to exits several km from the city, and clay pipes in its walls suggest water was supplied from outside in wartime. Its last resident was Demir Pasha.

row.old_value: A stone circle on Burley Moor that may actually be a ring cairn — the distinction is still debated. Large cairns including the Skirtful of Stones lie nearby.
row.new_value: On Burley Moor, twenty surviving stones set inside a low bank form Grubstones, an almost perfect circle about 10 metres across. Cairn circle, ring cairn or stone circle?

row.old_value: A pyramid of exactly 1,994 stone blocks was built over this grave in 1994 — the number matching the year. It is claimed to hold the legendary founder of the first Korean kingdom.
row.new_value: On the slope of Mount Taebak, a pyramid of 1994 stone blocks crowns the Mausoleum of Tangun, which North Korea claims as the tomb of the founder of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom.
Also called The Giant's Grave, Julliberrie's Grave is a long barrow near Chilham, probably raised in the fourth millennium BCE. A Romano-British coin hoard was later buried at its edge.

row.old_value: The site consists of at least 15 houses on an area of over 600 m2, with undercutting and subsequent demolitions that have continuously reduced the area.
row.new_value: Aghios Epiktitos Vrysi, at least 15 houses on a cliff 9 km east of Kyrenia, left awls and needles of a developed textile craft, and just one piece of obsidian, then extremely rare in Cyprus.

row.old_value: The site with images of llamas, vicuñas, felines, people and the sun lies near Lliwpa Pukyu at a height of 3,449 metres.
row.new_value: High in the Apurímac Region, at 3,449 metres, the petroglyphs of Llamachayuq, Quechua for 'with a little llama', show llamas, vicuñas, felines, people and the sun.

row.old_value: The main sight on the small island is the Southcairn, a 20 metre long chambered cairn dating from approx. 3000 BC on whose stones one can find ancient carvings.
row.new_value: On a tiny uninhabited Orkney island, a trapdoor leads into the Holm of Papa Chambered Cairn, a 20 metre long communal tomb from approximately 3000 BC with ancient carvings on its stones.

row.old_value: 1st-century AD Roman water chambers beneath Toledo, discovered in 1628. One large arched gallery feeds three parallel vaulted galleries that once supplied thermal baths at the Plaza de Amador.
row.new_value: Beneath Toledo, the Roman Remains under Alfonso X Street are arched galleries that fed water to a thermal bath from around the 1st century AD, hidden until 1628 and rediscovered in 1918.
Around 5500 BCE, the first settlers of Aigeira lived on its acropolis, leaving pottery that includes vessels likely used to make cheese. It was abandoned at the end of the Bronze Age.

row.old_value: Inca buildings cut into a granite cliff at 3,436 m altitude, used for both administration and religious ceremonies. The stonework hugs the rock face.
row.new_value: Amid grass-grown Inca terraces, Qollmay keeps a walled-off natural cavern with Inca-style stonework inside. Beside it, a rock like a birth canal, perhaps a place of fertility rituals.

row.old_value: Bronze Age burial mounds from the Cetina culture, named after the river valley. The Cetina people spread their burial customs across the Adriatic.
row.new_value: Mound fields line the valley slopes around Cetina, on a principal trade route from coast to hinterland, where the Cetina culture became dominant in the Early Bronze Age.

row.old_value: The artificial ring structures made of broken stalagmites now have been dated by uranium series dating as 176.5 thousand years old.
row.new_value: Deep in Bruniquel Cave, 336 metres from the entrance, lie rings of broken stalagmites dated as 176.5 thousand years old, with traces of fire. Researchers say early Neanderthals built them.

row.old_value: An early farming settlement from 6000 BC with layers from the Hassuna, Halaf, and Ubaid cultures. Three of Mesopotamia's earliest civilizations are stacked in one tell.
row.new_value: In the Sinjar valley, the hills of Yarim Tepe hold an early farming settlement going back to about 6000 BC, its lower levels yielding as many as 21 pieces of worked copper or copper ore.

row.old_value: Nine-terraced megalithic pyramid on the Cibedug River in West Java. Lebak Cibedug has menhirs and altars on each terrace, plus dolmens on site, a sacred complex in Banten regency's highland forest.
row.new_value: On the slope of Pasir Manggu hill in west Java, Lebak Cibedug Temple climbs in nine terraces of oval andesite stones, set with menhirs and altars, a design older than the temples of Bali.

row.old_value: Castle Goff is considered to be a "round": these are small circular embanked enclosures, with one entrance; they date from the late Iron Age to the early post-Roman period.
row.new_value: On a ridge between tributaries of the River Allen, Castle Goff is considered a round: a circular embanked enclosure about 60 metres across, its rampart rising 3.5 metres above the ditch.

row.old_value: Tappoch Broch, better known as Torwood Broch, is an iron-age broch located in a remote spot in dense woodland near Falkirk.
row.new_value: Deep in dense woodland near Falkirk lies Tappoch Broch, its paved oval chamber centred on a large fire spot, a short aisle leading to an unusually well-preserved staircase in the wall.

row.old_value: A 3rd-century AD summer capital of the Kingdom of Commagene, combining Greek and Persian architectural styles. A massive rock relief shows King Mithridates shaking hands with Heracles.
row.new_value: Arsemia Ören Yeri was a royal seat of Commagene. Besides Nemrut Dağı and Karakuş, a third hierothesion lies here: the burial site and cultic area of Mithridates, father of Antiochus.

row.old_value: A small circle of kerb stones that once surrounded a Bronze Age cairn. One stone bears rare spiral and concentric ring carvings — a type of art more common in Ireland than here.
row.new_value: Near Long Meg and Her Daughters lies Little Meg, a small circle of large kerb stones, one still bearing concentric circles and a spiral; at its centre a cist held bones and charcoal.

row.old_value: The walls of the chamber are 6 metres in height, while the corridor profile is 180 centimetres in height.
row.new_value: In the central Alentejo, the Great Dolmen of Comenda da Igreja hides a funerary chamber beneath a granite slab, its walls 6 metres high and its corridor just 180 centimetres tall.

row.old_value: 4th-century BC arch bridge discovered in 1966 near the eastern harbour of Rhodes. The oldest known voussoir arch bridge of the ancient world — a modest span that outlasted every empire that used it.
row.new_value: Near the Akandia Bay, the Rhodes Footbridge crosses an artificial canal on a surprisingly low arch of wedge-shaped poros stones: the oldest known Greek bridge with a voussoir arch.

row.old_value: The mound at Pirak rises 8 metres and covers 4.8 hectares in Balochistan. Occupation ran from 1800 to 800 BC near two related Indus-era sites along the Nari River.
row.new_value: In Balochistan, Pirak has some very early ironwork and iron artefacts. Its excavator dates the occupation from circa 1800 BCE to 800 BCE and records three phases of unbroken occupation.

row.old_value: Around 3000 BC. A Neolithic gallery grave of the Wartberg culture near Marburg — unique for its exceptionally rich ceramic assemblage. Its sunken rectangular chamber measured 5 x 2.2 metres.
row.new_value: In 1931 a farmer ploughing near Marburg encountered an obstacle: the Lohra Megalithic Tomb, a large main chamber with a small open antechamber, its dead cremated.

Stylized dolphins, cups and leaves hide in the complicated geometry of the Lopen Roman Mosaic, almost 7 metres square and laid in Blue Lias stone from the surrounding Somerset hills.

row.old_value: Caves with 120,000 years of continuous occupation — from Neanderthals to early modern humans. Thousands of fossils document the full transition between the two species.
row.new_value: In a limestone cliff above the river Samson, the Goyet Caves yielded 99 Neanderthal bones from at least five individuals, and their condition strongly suggests cannibalism.

row.old_value: 3000–2800 BC megalithic tholos tomb in Seville Province — found in 1868 but unexcavated for decades. Resumed in 1980 due to urban sprawl, Montelirio remains closed; objects now in Seville museum.
row.new_value: Radiocarbon dates on human bone suggest use of the Tholos de Montelirio began in 2875–2700 BC. The site is closed to the public, but its objects wait in the Archeological Museum of Seville.

row.old_value: The hill fort was refortified around 400, after the urban collapse associated with the withdrawal of Rome, and occupation extended into the sub-Roman period.
row.new_value: Overlooking Yatton, Cadbury Hill is crowned by an Iron Age hill fort where remains of round houses may still be seen. Around 400, after the withdrawal of Rome, it was refortified.

row.old_value: Dated on ceramics to around 100 BC, this multivallate Hampshire fort was reoccupied in the 13th–14th century. Medieval pottery sits alongside Iron Age ceramics in the same excavated levels.
row.new_value: In one of two infilled storage pits on King John's Hill lay a ring-headed pin fashioned from wire, in a small Hampshire hillfort of multiple defensive rings dated to approximately 100 BC.

row.old_value: The largest known open-air Aurignacian settlement site in western Eurasia, from the early Upper Palaeolithic -- when anatomically modern humans were first colonising Europe.
row.new_value: Mammoth, horse and reindeer remains lie at Breitenbach, currently the biggest open-air settlement in western Eurasia from the time anatomically modern humans first colonized Europe.

row.old_value: Positioned on a narrow ridge at 210 meters near Beaminster, with steep natural slopes for defense. The Wessex Ridgeway passes just north of the summit, placing it on a major ancient route.
row.new_value: On Waddon Hill in Dorset, its name Old English for wheat hill, the Second Legion under Vespasian built a short-lived Roman fort on a narrow ridge with steep natural slopes.

row.old_value: The site is made up of an array of deeply incised rock carvings that cover up to a height of 9 feet, a perpendicular rock face that is over 100 feet long and 75 feet high.
row.new_value: In the rain forest of Manú National Park, the rock face of Pusharo bears deeply incised heart-shaped faces, spirals, zigzags, suns and shapes that defy verbal description.

row.old_value: A carved swastika-like design from around 3300 BC—millennia before the symbol gained modern associations. It closely matches a motif found in Scandinavia.
row.new_value: On Woodhouse Crag, Ilkley Moor, the Swastika Stone bears a double-outlined swastika with a cup mark in each curved arm: the only one of its kind known in Britain, not verifiably dated.

row.old_value: 450 BC–1200 AD Buddhist stupa on a mound near Tando Muhammad Khan. Locally called the Tower of Sudheran — believed by some to be a cinerary stupa containing the ashes of the dead.
row.new_value: On a mound bearing the remains of a big ancient city in Sindh stands Sudheran-Jo-Thul, a Buddhist stupa south of Hyderabad that locals know as the Tower of Sudheran.

row.old_value: A cave with 15,000-year-old engravings showing detailed human faces with individual features. These realistic portraits challenged the idea that Ice Age art was only abstract.
row.new_value: Beside the Petit Moulin river, Léon Péricard found the paintings of La Marche Cave in November 1937, and five years of study with Stephane Lwoff revealed etchings on more than 1,500 slabs.

row.old_value: A stoa to Zeus Eleutherios built around 425 BC—a rare cult center rather than a marketplace. It was founded to celebrate freedom after the Persian War.
row.new_value: In the Ancient Agora of Athens stood the Stoa of Zeus, dedicated to Zeus Eleutherios, a cult founded after the Persian War. Researchers think Mnesikles may have built it.

row.old_value: A stone row stretching across Ringmoor Down, paired with a cairn circle. Dartmoor holds the densest concentration of stone rows in the world.
row.new_value: On Ringmoor Down in Devon, the Ringmoor Stone Row and Cairn Circle runs 356 metres, from a standing stone at its northern end to a cairn circle 12.6 metres across.
On the narrowest part of a small plateau near Casaglione, the dolmen of Tremeca rests on four rough-hewn granite blocks capped with a slab, its opening turned toward the southeast.

row.old_value: One of Europe's best-preserved mithraea, this underground temple to the sun god Mithra imitates a cave. It is now protected inside a glass-walled cage.
row.new_value: Found by chance in 1931 during digging for a house, the Jajce Mithraeum is a temple of Mithraism from the early 4th century, perhaps even the 2nd, and among Europe's best-preserved sites.

row.old_value: Third-millennium BC copper smelting community in Huelva, achieving furnace temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. It provides very early evidence of copper metallurgy in Atlantic Europe.
row.new_value: Excavations at Cabezo Juré in Alosno, Andalusia, have laid bare the vestiges of an ancient community of workers specialized in copper metallurgy, active between 2873 and 2274 BC.

row.old_value: A Roman buttress dam over 600 meters long but less than 5 meters high. It served double duty: irrigating farmland and supplying water to the nearby town.
row.new_value: On the River Amarguillo lie the ruins of the Consuegra Dam, a Roman buttress dam of the 3rd or 4th century AD: less than 5 metres high, yet remarkably long, over 600 metres.

row.old_value: A submerged Mesolithic settlement in 11 metres of water, discovered when a lobster was seen tossing worked flint tools from its burrow. Dates to around 6000 BC.
row.new_value: In approximately 11 metres of water off the Isle of Wight lies Bouldnor Cliff, a settlement of about 8,000 years ago: burnt flints, mounds of timbers and pits, preserved under silt and mud.

row.old_value: Just north of the ridge summit of Cefn Bryn, there is a Neolithic burial ground, known as "Arthur's Stone".
row.new_value: On Cefn Bryn, a ridge in the heart of the Gower Peninsula, over sixty cairns have been found beneath the bracken, and just north of its summit lies a Neolithic burial ground, Arthur's Stone.

row.old_value: Three temples built to honour Enki, the Sumerian god of wisdom and fresh water. A natural spring inside the temple held deep spiritual significance for Dilmun worshippers.
row.new_value: Three temples rise one atop another at the Barbar Temple, the oldest from 3000 BC, thought built to worship Enki, god of wisdom and freshwater. Its most famous find: a copper bull's head.

row.old_value: Portal dolmen from 3000 BC near Camborne -- locally called the "Giant Frying Pan." Collapsed in 1966 and re-erected in 2014, making it the only restored dolmen of its type in Cornwall.
row.new_value: Also known as the Giant's Frying Pan, Carwynnen Quoit is a portal dolmen built around 3000 BC. It collapsed in 1966 and was re-erected in 2014; the dolmen weighs around 10 tons.

row.old_value: Saka Iron Age kurgan necropolis covering 430 hectares on the outskirts of Almaty, with 47 burial mounds from the 5th to 3rd centuries BC. Declared a protected monument in 2010.
row.new_value: In Almaty, 47 Saka mounds spread across 430 hectares, the largest at the centre 14 meters high and 100 meters wide: the Boralday Archaeological Site, an early Iron Age kurgan necropolis.

row.old_value: Among the most significant rock art discoveries in the world, ranked in the top 10 finds of 2021. Twenty-one carvings -- 17 camels, two equids, and one unidentified figure -- on a remarkable scale.
row.new_value: In the Al-Jawf region, the Camel Carving Site likely holds the oldest known surviving large-scale animal reliefs in the world, Neolithic work unlike the rock art common in Saudi Arabia.

row.old_value: A tor with a Neolithic enclosure, Bronze Age hut circles, and a summit Logan Stone. Four millennia of human activity stacked on one hilltop.
row.new_value: Rough stone walls ring the summit of Rough Tor on Bodmin Moor, once a Neolithic enclosure. On its southern slopes, stone hut circles gather around enclosures that may have held stock.

row.old_value: A sanctuary on the Acropolis dedicated to Aglauros, a princess who threw herself from the cliffs to save the city. Young Athenian soldiers swore their oaths here.
row.new_value: On the Acropolis in Athens, the Aglaureion honoured Aglauros, daughter of King Cecrops, believed to have sacrificed herself here to protect the city from invasion.

row.old_value: A cave with bones of woolly mammoth, rhinoceros, and reindeer alongside Neanderthal flint tools. Human use spans from the Middle Paleolithic through the Upper Paleolithic.
row.new_value: In the valley of the Little Krems, Gudenus Cave held bones of woolly mammoth and woolly rhinoceros, flint tools and a fragment of a bone flute dated to about 16,000–10,000 BCE.

row.old_value: A 52-metre-long Neolithic barrow with a 1.8-metre standing stone placed just 9 metres away. The pairing of barrow and menhir suggests a deliberate ritual connection between them.
row.new_value: On a ridge overlooking valleys, Lyneham Long Barrow stretches 52 metres near a 1.8-metre-tall standing stone; later, two Anglo-Saxon burials were cut into the top of its mound.

row.old_value: A perforated sarsen stone that produces a booming sound when blown through its natural holes. Legend says King Alfred used it to summon troops against the Danes.
row.new_value: Blow into one of its holes the right way and the Blowing Stone, a perforated sarsen in Oxfordshire, booms. Legend says King Alfred summoned his troops with it for the Battle of Ashdown.

row.old_value: Built early in the 2nd century AD and partly rebuilt around 200 AD, this Cumbria fort has a diamond shape unique along Hadrian's Wall — adapted to hilltop terrain while guarding nearby lead mining.
row.new_value: Whitley Castle, the highest stone-built Roman fort in Britain, is lozenge-shaped to fit the site. Its finds include altars to Hercules and Apollo and a bronze handle shaped like a dolphin.

row.old_value: Harappan outpost on the Makran coast, occupied 2600–1900 BC, about 24 km north of Pasni. Its coastal position aligns with evidence for Bronze Age overseas maritime commerce.
row.new_value: Its name means burnt hill: Sokhta Koh, a Harappan site near Pasni, lies strewn with hundreds of thousands of potsherds, and scores of open pit ovens for firing the pottery can still be seen.

row.old_value: A double pyramid with twin shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. It was rebuilt six times, each layer encasing the last like a nesting doll.
row.new_value: Tenayuca holds the earliest Aztec double pyramid yet found. A double stairway climbs to where the temples of Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli once stood, above a wall of serpents.

row.old_value: A large upright granite stone sometimes called a menhir, though it may be naturally positioned. Its name translates to "Lovers' Rock."
row.new_value: A granite stone shaped like a mushroom, more than two meters high: at the Rocha dos Namorados, girls of marriageable age still consult the rock to learn how long until they marry.

row.old_value: A Neolithic holed stone 2.3 m tall with a 43 cm hole near its base — the largest of its type in Cornwall. It was moved to its present spot in 1847.
row.new_value: Near Gweek stands the Tolvan Holed Stone, the largest holed stone in Cornwall: a triangular stone 2.3 m high, pierced near its base by a hole approximately 43 cm in diameter.

In 1940 a cranium nearly 15,000 years old came to light at the Keilor Archaeological Site. Hearths about 31,000 years BP; megafauna remains suggest a possible Aboriginal hunting link.
Lakhmir Mound rises in the Naig Valley of Sindh as a conical hill above a lower section resembling a town, where black-on-red pottery of the Indus Valley civilization lies scattered.

row.old_value: In 1940 a cranium nearly 15,000 years old came to light at the Keilor Archaeological Site. Hearths about 31,000 years BP; megafauna remains suggest a possible Aboriginal hunting link.
Lakhmir Mound rises in the Naig Valley of Sindh as a conical hill above a lower section resembling a town, where black-on-red pottery of the Indus Valley civilization lies scattered.
